additional_requirements: Functioning is not markedly impaired apart from the impact of the delusion(s) or its ramifications

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.

subtypes.Persecutory Delusions: The false belief that one is being harmed or monitored by other people or organizations.
subtypes.Referential Delusions: The conviction that ordinary events, remarks, or behaviors have specific relevance to oneself.
subtypes.Grandiose Delusions: The false belief that one possesses special abilities, power, or fame.
subtypes.Erotomanic Delusions: The false belief that another person is in love with or has affection for them.
subtypes.Nihilistic Delusions: A destructive or negative conviction that the world is ending or that a major catastrophe will occur.
subtypes.Somatic Delusions: The baseless conviction that there is a serious abnormality with one's body or organs.
subtypes.Jealous Delusions: The conviction that one's spouse or romantic partner is being unfaithful without sufficient evidence.

symptom.disease_info: Delusional disorder is characterized by the presence of one or more non-bizarre or plausible-sounding delusions lasting at least one month, in the relative absence of other psychotic features such as prominent hallucinations, disorganized speech, or marked negative symptoms. Outside of the delusional beliefs, cognitive functioning and behavior are often largely preserved, and overall functioning may remain relatively intact compared with schizophrenia. The content of the delusions can be persecutory, somatic, grandiose, jealous, or erotomanic, and individuals often come to clinical attention because of interpersonal conflict, occupational problems, or legal/organizational involvement stemming from their fixed beliefs. The course tends to be chronic, with limited insight and resistance to contrary evidence, distinguishing it from overvalued ideas or mood-congruent beliefs seen in major mood disorders.

patient.stressor: About a year ago, after his second unsuccessful attempt at securing a major research grant and watching a younger colleague get a coveted faculty position, Coleman began to fixate on the idea that a small group in his department’s grant review committee had decided to block his career advancement. Initially, this surfaced as frustrated comments about academic politics during late-night brewing sessions and hikes, but over time the conviction solidified: he started attributing minor scheduling changes, delayed email replies, and neutral feedback on his teaching to a coordinated effort to sideline him. Despite continuing to perform adequately as a teaching assistant and maintaining his hobbies, he increasingly withdrew from departmental social events, avoided certain collaborators, and spent long evenings combing through funding announcements and committee rosters trying to "prove" the pattern he saw. His spouse eventually persuaded him to see a psychiatrist after he refused an offer to co-author a paper—insisting it was a trap to discredit him—and came home from a faculty meeting visibly upset that "everyone was pretending" not to acknowledge the supposed conspiracy.
patient.chief_complaint: “I know a few people in my department have quietly agreed to block my grants and promotions, and I can’t shake that belief no matter how much my wife or colleagues argue with me.”
